speechtext:
On that I agree with the hon. member.	I think one of the best
speeches made since the beginning of the session was that made in another debate about the Japanese by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud). I speak as one who comes from the part of the country where there are the largest number of broad-minded people. I refer to the province of Quebec where no discrimination exists against any one. The people of my province have proved that on many occasions by electing English-speaking gentlemen in French-speaking constituencies. They were satisfied with them so long as they were satisfied with their policies. This should be known to all. On those occasions the province of Quebec proved to be broad-minded and without prejudice.
I wonder if this question of immigration is being considered as it should be. We are now discussing this bill and then we shall deal with the bill on housing. In my view we should have first settled the matter of housing and then we could see what we could do for immigrants. If we have no houses in which to shelter them when they come the

Immigration Act
situation may be quite embarrassing. The housing problem is far from being settled in spite of the splendid efforts of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). It is strange that when we discuss certain matters we consider first that which should be in the second place, and this is one example.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke a few days ago about immigration he said that transportation was limited. That is true, but transportation is not the main problem in connection with immigration. Transportation is a secondary problem; the main problem is that of selection. The hon. member who just spoke said that race should not be a consideration when the qualification of an immigrant was under review. He is perfectly right. There should be no question of race at all; the only question should be whether or not the newcomer will prove an asset to Canada. If a man has a good background; if he is willing to come to Canada and consider Canada as his country, then he should be admitted. It is only after that inspection has taken place that we should consider the transportation of that man and his family to this country.
We should not forget that the old pioneers of French as well as of British extraction were simply immigrants to this country. Champlain was an immigrant. Jacques Cartier was not; he was a navigator. Monseigneur de Laval, the first Quebec bishop, was an immigrant. He belonged to a noble family in France and was a chaplain at the French court. He could have done very well over there but he came here as an immigrant. So did many people of British extraction, but they decided to come and settle in this country, do their share in developing it and raise their children here. We are all the same. We have only to consider who the first pioneers in this country were to realize that we are all descendants of our ancestors who, the moment they decided to come here, made Canada the country of their choice. So I say that we are all descendants of immigrants, and we have no reason to be ashamed of that. It is the same in all the British dominions. In Australia, New Zealand and Africa, all the white people are descendants of those who went there from various parts of Europe, settled in those dominions and helped in their development.
At times we, hear it said that we should have no immigrants. That is the point of view of some people, and while we may differ from it we must respect their right to their point of view. Any immigration we have should be selected immigration, selected at the source,
and we should do nothing in our immigration policy just to please another nation. I do not see how our immigration policy should be related to the social, political and economic circumstances of other countries, even if those circumstances resulted from the war. We should consider the conditions in our own country and in each case we should consider the effect of the admission of one immigrant and his family to this country. How can we fix any quota on immigration now and say that we shall bring in so many displaced persons, one thousand, two thousand, five thousand, one hundred thousand, unless they are all examined in the first place to see whether they will be an asset to Canada if they do come here?
We are not far away from the last war and there is still prejudice against some peoples of European countries with whom we have been at war. I understand that these effects of war last quite a long time. During the war we heard so much propaganda against the peoples of central Europe that we are still under the impression that they might make bad citizens and that we must ban their entry into Canada.
In Europe so many people have suffered deeply during the war and post-war that they want to get away from Europe. They want to go to another country where they can enjoy a liberty which they have not known in Europe for a very long time, scores and scores of years. They say: We will go to America or Canada, where life is different, where people enjoy liberty. That is a great tribute to our country. But in the first place, to those who have suffered from the evils of both wars in Europe and to those who have suffered from hunger and cold and from the lack of shelter we must show the conditions which they will experience in Canada and tell them how they can make good in this country. For instance, if Canada is described to. them as a land of liberty, as a true democracy, they will be greatly surprised to find controls in force in this country when they come here. We must not disappoint them. We should- tell them the truth about this country. Advertisements should not be used only to promote the interests of transportation companies, rail and water. There should be no exaggeration in thfe advertisements; the people should be told the plain facts about Canada. They should be told about our mode of living, and as far as possible

and I believe this is possible-we should aim to admit only those who have the same mentality as our own.
I have no prejudice against Chinese women, although no one in Canada will contend that the majority of Chinese women have the culture of Madame Chiang. It is a serious mat-
Immigration Act

ter to open the door too wide to Asiatic peoples, because their mode of living is entirely different from ours and they may be miserable after they get into this country. That is not a matter of discrimination at all. I just put it to hon. gentlemen: Is the education of Chinese women the same as that of white women? It is entirely different, and perhaps Chinese women would be disappointed when they got here. That is an angle of the question to which I draw the attention of my hon. friend.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is what Ontario people say about the residents of Quebec.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I will not compare them with Chinese women, but I will say that their education is much more like that of the residents of Quebec than is the education of the Chinese and I am sure my hon. friend will admit that, although he is a great humourist at times.
I can understand that the people of Europe who have suffered so much not only physically but mentally now want a change, and if they break their family ties and get away from the traditions which they have so long cherished in their native land, whether it be the British isles, France, Germany or any other country, it is because they want something different. They want to come to a country where they can breathe. I hope no one of them will be disappointed when they come to Canada; that here they will enjoy liberty and the respect of their fellow citizens, provided that there is room for them here. So long as we have a certain number of unemployed I do not see how we can bring into this country people from outside who will do at lower rates work which does not exist for our own people. The standard1 of life in Canada is higher than the average standard of life of people under similar conditions in Europe. Therefore our . people need more to live on than do Europeans. Asiatic people need less to live on than do Europeans.
If our own people suffer from unemployment for any consideration, because there is less work, ljecause the company cannot afford to keep a certain personnel, et cetera, et cetera, they have to say at home receiving the benefits from the unemployment insurance commission. What will they think of immigrants coming to this country by the shipload to take their places in jobs, in plants, in any kind of work?
It creates discontent, and discontent breeds many troubles.
It is not the question of race which should be the subject matter of the inspection of immigrants; it should be the background. The

inspectors should be qualified men to consider not only the physical health of those who want to come to Canada but also their mentality, because those who come here as subversive agents are the most dangerous of all, and Ottawa is a place for spies. We know about it. We were all put to shame on account of it. But there is something else. It is common knowledge that a woman who was under the roof of the high commissioner for the United Kingdom was a pink communist since 1932. She was there under the wing of all the high commissioners who succeeded each other, spying for another country.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: What is her name? '

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
My friend knows as much about the matter as I do. I will not insist upon it. He knows about it. I am stating a fact which is public; it is not secret, and it has been announced in the press. Those who do spying, subversive propaganda and others may be wolves disguised as lambs to get into this country and create trouble. Therefore the check must not be on the race; the check must be on the person who is coming here. That is one point which I wish to bring to the attention of the house.
Moreover, sir, what shall we do with the mass of immigrants who may come to this country? Will they be farmers? There is no room for them. There is very little room left for farms in the St. Lawrence valley, in the Ottawa valley or in the west. The best lands have been taken. The only thing to do is to develop the north and bring selected immigrants to the north. But, first, the north should be opened. We should have railways to go there. There should be surveys of land. Make a choice of the best possible land, the most fertile land. We should send prospectors to the north to develop the mines. Can one expect the immigrants to live as the first pioneers did who came to this country, and go to the north in a canoe and portage and all that? We should have roads for them. Therefore, unless there are better communication facilities with the north, I do not see how we can have mass immigration into this country. There is great wealth in the north. According to the explorers, including the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who spends so usefully his leisure time during the summer in visiting the far north, there is unsuspected wealth in the north. These are elementary considerations. If we are to bring immigrants to this country the coming of each of them should be such an asset to the country that he will repay Canada in some way or another by being a country builder.

Immigration Act
If we have some difficulty it is precisely because the matter is not considered seriously enough. Some people would like to have only citizens of British countries come here. They know very well that in every British country, as in ours, there are citizens who belong to other races. I shall ask my hon. friends from the western provinces who are the best farmers that they have there. They will answer me quite rightly that there are some who are of every origin. If they take a farmer from central Europe, Hungarians and others, they will realize that they are progressive and they make a success of their farms. The same thing applies to those who come from countries nearer Russia, people from Germany, Italy and from all over Europe. Generally they do very well, and I do not see why they should be banned from this country when they would be an asset to Canada if they were admitted here.
I bring all these matters to the attention of the minister. He is an able man; he is gifted with that rare quality of common sense. I believe, too, that he is a good Canadian, notwithstanding the fact that he was not born in Canada. He is a much better Canadian than some who were born here, as I said to him also when he occupied the Chair.
We may naturally consider the question of refugees and displaced persons with Christian charity. We must do that, but the government should not be a benevolent society to assist all those who have suffered in Europe. It is a physical impossibility to do that. Because a man has suffered in Europe, it does not follow that he will become a good Canadian citizen. There must be something more than that. The fact that a man or woman is a refugee is not a qualification for admittance to Canada; not at all. But that is not to say that, because one is a refugee, he shall not be admitted to Canada with full honour if he has the necessary qualifications to show that he will be a good citizen and will live up to the expectations of the minister, the government and the population of this country.
I come now to the practical steps which may be taken within the present physical limitations imposed by transportation, and I say that we should not complain and say that the transportation facilities are not as good as they were previously. My reason for saying that is that it gives the minister the time in which to shape a policy of immigration. He may call it planning if he wishes; that is his own business. But it should be a well-thought-out and well-inspired policy. I do not believe in too great a moral obligation to assist other peoples of the world 83166-176
unless the people of Canada are well looked after and there is no unemployment in this country, at least in the technical trades. Assistance may be given individually by those who wish to do something; but, with the burden of taxation that we have, I do not see that as a nation we can any longer come to the assistance of the other countries of the world, especially when they snub Canada whenever she has a suggestion to make at the various meetings or conferences. If I say that, it is not because I have no Christian charity; it is because I think of my own people before thinking of others. I may be called a nationalist, but I believe that Canada is a country which exists and that Canadians should be looked after first; then, if we have something left over, we shall help others. I say that charity begins at home.
The Prime Minister mentioned some thousands who were coming here for early admission. What is the number? I will ask the minister these questions and he may answer me later. What will be the quota that Canada will accept as its share in meeting the general problem of immigration? What are the measures of productive immigration, and what is productive immigration as mentioned by the Prime Minister in his statement the other day? He said also the essential thing is that immigrants be selected and that their numbers be adjusted to the absorptive capacity of the country. What is the absorptive capacity of the country? How many immigrants can we accept, and where? They will land in Halifax, Montreal, Quebec city or Vancouver, but where will they go afterwards? That is not an academic matter. If a man, a woman and their children decide to come to Canada, it will probably be with the definite purpose of settling here. Therefore we should be ready to receive them just the same as when we invite them through the officers of the Department of Mines and Resources. They will be the guests of Canada until they settle down. But no one invites guests until he is able to offer them shelter and hospitality. That is the thing to think about, and I find that until now the discussion has been theoretical and vague; there has been nothing definite about what will be done with the immigrants after they have arrived in this country If Canada does not live up to their expectations, we shall be severely judged by them, and they will be right. They will have the right to blame the government and the people of this country for not delivering the goods when those immigrants come here.
I have tried to make a moderate speech, but this is a matter that I have been thinking

Immigration Act

about for a long time. I am not opposed to the change with regard to the Chinese, but China is a country which is still at war with the communists. How can we make the distinction between a Chinaman who is a communist and a Chinaman who is not a communist? To us, they all look alike. In addition to that, the admission of Chinese will perhaps be one means of the infiltration of communism into this country. We are not at war with China; they were our allies during the war. Part of that immense country of China was our ally, but the other part is at war with our ally. Whether they are supported by another country, I do not know; I presume so. But they are communists. If the minister seeks to prevent the admission of communist Chinese men or women, it will be very easy- in fact, easier for them than for anybody else -to defraud the inspectors and put it over them. When I say that, it is not because I hold any feeling of discrimination against the Chinese but because I think of the future. I do not want any communists, whether Chinese or white, to come to this country. That is my point of view. The same situation prevails among the populations of Europe. There are communists among the British people, just the same as there are among peoples of different racial origin in the other countries of Europe. Suppose we have to admit one who is a communist, or a pink communist, such as one who came on an official mission not long ago; the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) fixed him up, and I tried to do my best too. He was admitted with full honours. I need not name him, which would only give him more publicity, but he came to this country, paraded here, and was very well received. We even had him at the parliamentary restaurant upstairs, where he made a little speech. He was a pink communist, but was welcomed here.
I leave all these considerations with the minister and trust that with his usual good judgment he will make the best of the problem. With his usual care and patriotism I am sure he will see to it that immigration is not resumed for the sole benefit of the transportation companies or those whose business it is to secure permits for the newcomers. This debate has been conducted on a high plane, and I hope it may continue so. I hope this important question of immigration will be scrutinized carefully by all members of parliament, just as it is considered very deeply by the Canadian people at large.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
In opening my remarks upon this subject, Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer my congratu-

lations to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), to whose speech on Friday last we listened with great attention. I think everyone in the chamber must have been greatly impressed with his grasp of the subject and the sincerity with which he spoke, a sincerity due, I feel sure, to the personal knowledge he gained through an inspection of conditions in the displaced persons camps in Europe. I want to join with the hon. member in expressing fear lest this great announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-great although a year or two years late-may not be followed up by that energetic action which is necessary to translate into something concrete, a good policy, wanted by the whole country for a long time. So far we have had only the word; we have only gotten over the first hump, that of deciding that we are going to increase the population of this country through immigration. As yet we have not gotten down to the equally important business of translating that word into vigorous action. When the Prime Minister spoke he indicated that such action was contemplated. I want to express my hope that it will not be necessary for various groups of interested people and members of parliament to exercise the same pressure that has been required to bring the government over the first hurdle they had to surmount. In dealing with this subject the Prime Minister said, at page 2645 of Hansard:
The government is strongly of the view that our immigration policy should be devised in a positive sense, with the definite objective, as I have already stated, of enlarging the population of the country. This it will seek to attain through the development and energetic application of productive immigration measures.
We shall attempt to hold the government strictly to that statement, and see to it that they do adopt the energetic measures they promise. There is very much to be done before this decision, great as it is, can be translated into effective action. The necessary action does not lie only abroad, in the opening up of new immigration offices and making some special arrangements with regard to these refugees who so greatly desire to come to Canada. If we are to bring a large number of immigrants to this country over a period of years a great deal must be done internally if we are to absorb sufficient numbers to carry out the purpose laid down by the Prime Minister. It will require considerable cooperation between the government, industry and labour. It will require negotiations with other governments. Above all it will require a large capital development of our natural resources, so that we may put people to work and give them a stake before they go on the-

Immigration Act
land, as we probably hope most of them will do. We shall have to look to the north; we must see how we can stimulate prospecting and' the mining industry generally, so that we can be sure of an ever-expanding number of jobs for people coming to this country. In a smaller compass we shall have to think in terms of assisted passages, special ships, and so on.
Then we must not overlook- one important means of fostering immigration, to which I should now like to refer shortly; that is the scheme exemplified by the Fairbridge farm school near Duncan on Vancouver island. I am sure the minister knows about that scheme, but for the benefit of others who may not, let me say that it is a school set up for the training in Canadian ways of young boys and girls brought in from the British isles. The general policy of the school is set out in the principal's report for last year:
It is to settle in Canada boys and girls of British origin, selected in England and approved by Canadian immigration authorities. The interpretation of the word "settle" by this administration is to give the children such education and training under conditions of home care as will fit them to earn their own living as responsible Canadian citizens.
I want now to read another important paragraph in order to bring the crux of the matter to the attention of the house and particularly to the attention of the minister:
The extent of the education so given depends entirely on the funds available for that purpose whether supplied by the British isles or by Canada.
The school has been in operation for over eleven years, and has been very successful during that time, though all along it has been plagued by lack of funds; and it has not had any assistance from the dominion government. As at December 31, 1946, its strength was sixty boys and twenty-one girls. When it was designed I understood that its establishment was supposed to be fixed at 250. The difference,
I suggest to the minister, is accounted for principally by the fact that funds for a much larger establishment have not been available. When one is considering the value of such schemes it is interesting to refer to the disposition of the graduates of the school in those eleven years. Of the male graduates, twenty-five per cent are now engaged in agriculture in Canada while four per cent are in occupations related to agriculture. Some twenty-one per cent are serving in the merchant service. We know' how important that contribution was to our war effort. Then in industry and in business we have a further twenty-five per cent. The remainder are classified under manufacturing and building students, armed forces trades and miscellaneous. Of the girl 83166-1764
graduates fifty-two per cent are engaged in applied home economics, twenty-six per cent are housewives and the remainder are classified under sales and service, business and nursing, manufacturing and miscellaneous. It will be noted that the majority of the graduates from this school have gone into occupations in Canada to which we sorely need recruits, and they have amply justified the purposes for which the Fairbridge school was established.
When one turns to the war record of the graduates, he finds it very good indeed. At the termination of hostilities with Japan, ninety-five per cent of the boys and thirty-six per cent of the girls eligible by age to volunteer to serve, had done so. I do not suppose that record has been exceeded by any other institution or group in Canada.
For this, school funds have been provided from two- sources. Two-thirds are provided from Great Britain, and one-third comes from private donations by Canadian citizens, and by the British Columbia government.
The sums necessary to carry on the work for 1946 were divided as follows: private donations from Canada, $16,553, and a provincial grant of $12,500. making a total from Canada of about $29,000. From England the amount was $69,384. If this school is to be carried on- in the future, and is to continue to make the contribution it has made toward training young people in Canadian ways and customs, it is urgently necessary that it be given further financial assistance in Canada. It becomes increasingly difficult to get funds from Great Britain and the total funds available have not been enough to fill up the establishment originally intended. There is a great field for the minister, not only in this one school on Vancouver island, but in the establishment of other schools operating on similar principles in other parts of Canada-.
One of the energetic steps the minister could now take would be to look into this question of schools for the training of child immigrants in Canadian ways, and seeing to it that we have a continuous source of new Canadians brought in, in their tender years. There are many countries which at the present time are not willing to give up their manpower; but they would not mind making the young children available, if their parents wished them to come, so that they might have an opportunity for a greater future in this country. I hope the minister will take under his serious consideration, this particular scheme, and schemes of this kind, and perhaps make them one of his first energetic steps.
Immigration Act

I wish now to turn to the matter of oriental immigration-Chinese immigration-for the sole purpose of refreshing the minister's mind, on the questions asked by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) when he spoke on Friday afternoon. I am anxious to hear the answers to these questions when the minister closes the debate, because they are most important to the people of British Columbia.
Dealing with the subject, the Prime Minister said this:
I wish to make it quite clear that Canada is perfectly within her rights in selecting the persons whom we regard as desirable future citizens. It is not a "fundamental human right ' of any alien to enter Canada. It is a privilege. It is a matter of domestic policy. Immigration is subject to the control of the parliament of Canada.
Those words will be most reassuring to the people of British Columbia. The Prime Minister went on to say that the Chinese Immigration Act was to be repealed upon the grounds of a seeming discrimination against our ally, China. I would join him in any attempt to remove any possible idea that Canada discriminates against that or any other country which was our ally in the war. But at the same time I wish to point out to the minister that the step we are taking in repealing this act, despite the clear enunciation of our policy, namely, that we have control over our own immigration, is a serious step for the house to take.
The Chinese Immigration Act, which was passed in 1923, was not put upon the statute oooks suddenly, but was enacted only after many years of effort on the part of those who were facing the practical problems we have heard discussed at such great length. We are now breaking down a safeguard which has existed on the statute books for twenty-four [DOT] years, one which has been most important to many people in British Columbia. I shall not go into detail on that point, because I think it has been fully covered in debate. However, under the measure now before the house it would be possible, simply by the repeal of this act, for the Chinese population in Canada to be tripled.
If members from British Columbia are to justify the letting go of this safeguard, not only must they be told the policy of the government as stated by the Prime Minister, with which I am sure most of us agree, but they must be told also the practical results they may expect from the application of that policy. We must not be left in the position where we do not know what will flow from what we do today. We want to know, in par-

ticular, if this is really a friendly gesture to our ally, or if it involves a major change in practice.
With that in mind I would refer now to the questions asked by the hon. member for Kamloops. First of all, what is the situation with regard to the treaty with China? Have negotiations been broken off? Are they continuing? If they are continuing, do they include the subject of immigration? What relationship has the repeal of this act to the negotiations for a treaty with China?
Second, how many Chinese does the minister expect will come to Canada in 1947, 1948 and 1949 as a result of this policy? Will the policy permit wives of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin to be brought in when the marriage occurs after the date of the repeal of the act? I understand that we calculate .most of our estimates of future population in relation to the year 1971, and I should like to know if the minister could make any forecast of what the Chinese population of Canada will be in that year and as a result of this policy?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been interested in immigration for quite a number of years, and in

Immigration Act
the first speech which I made in this chamber in 1945 I made a plea to the government to adopt a large-scale immigration policy for Canada to be put into effect immediately our service men who were then overseas had been repatriated. Thus I was happy to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announce, on Thursday last, an immigration policy of considerable extent. It was one of the few government announcements which I have heard with which I was in entire agreement. In fact it would appear that the government had been studying our party's policy on this matter and had decided to adopt it. Be that as it may, they have seen the light and I trust that the policy as announced will be carried out energetically. I would have been even happier with the Prime Minister's announcement if he had outlined specific means by which the policy was to be carried out. However that is an omission which the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) will probably correct when he makes his speech.
In connection with displaced persons in Europe, I hope that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), as reported on page 2736 of Hansard, will be adopted and carried out by the government. He suggested that immigration offices be set up in Germany, Austria and Italy where these displaced persons are to be found. I agree thoroughly with him, because there is no use in setting up offices in places where displaced persons are not living. If we are to help these people by bringing in a considerable number as settlers, immigration offices must be located where they are or immigration officers must go to them. It is manifestly impossible for them to go to the immigration offices.
In this connection I should like to make a plea for the Balts, the former citizens of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. I understand that these people constitute the largest single group in the displaced' persons camps in Germany. I understand also that a certain number of these people are of German extraction and, as the regulations stand at present, they would not be considered suitable immigrants to this country. I should like the government to wipe out or to pay no attention to that regulation which, I think, was made by some international organization having to do with moving these people out of Germany. I am sure that many of these people would make the best type of citizen. There is no question that a considerable proportion of our population of German origin have proved excellent settlers in this country, and I do not think
we should hold the fact that they happen to be of that particular ethnic origin against these people and refuse to let them enter.
A considerable number of refugees are without relatives in Canada, and I have no doubt that many of these people are of the best type in the refugee camps. I hope that the policy as announced by the Prime Minister of bringing out relatives of persons now in Canada or workers for primary industries will not be carried out so as to exclude some of the best of the refugees in the displaced persons camps. I would much sooner bring out people who would make good1 citizens, who would make outstanding contributions to the life of this country, whether or not they have relatives here, than I would bring out a poorer type of refugee who happens to have relatives here. The suitability of the person and the contribution which he can make to this country should be overriding considerations when we are dealing with refugees.
The government gave financial assistance to the bringing out of certain Polish soldiers to this country, and I took it from the Prime Minister's statement that similar financial assistance would be given to some of the displaced persons now in Europe. I have no quarrel with that, but I should like to ask the minister whether the moneys which have been expended to bring out the Polish soldiers are considered as loans which they will be required1 to repay, or considered as outright gifts. My view is that they should be considered as loans, and I think the same thing should apply to the cost of bringing out refugees from Europe under the newly announced policy.
Financial assistance should, in my opinion, be extended in even greater measure to immigrants from the British isles. They follow our way of life; they have essentially the same laws and particularly they speak the same language. As a result, they are assimilated almost immediately upon arriving in Canada. In my view, one of the chief things to look for in selecting immigrants, no matter where they come from, is how readily they can be assimilated into the life of this country. There is not the slightest doubt that the people of the British isles can be assimilated much more rapidly than those from any other land, and therefore they should be given the preference. And so, Mr. Speaker, I say that when financial assistance is being given to people from any other country a greater measure of it should be given to assist people from the British isles. I am not advocating that the assistance should be in the form of straight grants but, if a system of repayable loans were put into operation to assist people
Immigration Act

of the British isles to come to this country, you would have a large number of applicants. Undoubtedly at the present time millions of people in the British isles are anxious to emigrate, but a very large number of them have not the financial means to do so, particularly in view of the extremely high cost of ocean transport. I would strongly urge upon the government that consideration be given to a scheme of financial assistance to assist immigrants from the British isles.
I do not know whether the government have on foot any scheme or schemes to secure transport, which has been one of the big bottlenecks in bringing anybody to this country. If they have, before they bring anyone from Europe or anywhere else they should use some of that transport to bring to this country the fiancees of our own exservicemen. I know a considerable number in that class who are still in Europe. I have been working personally for over a year on the case of a well-to-do farmer just south of Calgary. During the war he was overseas and immediately upon his return he pleaded to get his fiancee brought out. Well over a year has passed, and the last I heard, some two weeks ago, was that his fiancee was still in England and unable to get transportation. To begin with, there was considerable delay because of the difficulties in getting all her papers in order. That is one thing which the immigration branch, now that its staff is to be increased, should iron out, so that people can get their papers quickly. There should be no delay on that score, but there was a considerable delay in her case.
Furthermore, when the government makes special provision for transportation, the very first people who should be brought out are the financees of our ex-servicemen. I have never been able to understand why fiancees were not included with wives in some modified form of the provisions which were made for bringing the dependents of our ex-servicemen back to this country.
I am in complete agreement with that part of the bill which deals with the bringing of dependents of ex-service men to Canada. But there are some cases of hardship caused by too strict and literal an interpretation of the act. and perhaps because of the wording of the act, which I find is interpreted literally.
I have another case on which I have been working for well over a year. It is that of a Canadian of Belgian extraction. He came to this country at the age of four with his parents. He returned to Belgium in 1931 and got married. He brought his wife back to Canada and lived here until shortly before

the war. They had a child and his wife and child went back to Belgium with him. He returned to Canada just before the war broke out, and she was to remain a few months longer and then join him, but she was caught by the German invasion of Belgium and remained behind the German lines throughout the war. This man joined the army in 1940 and was overseas for more than five years. He did not. get back to this country until January, 1946. He attempted to get his wife out under these provisions for bringing out dependents, wives and children, but was turned down because the act says that they must be dependents of men who were married overseas. He was not married overseas and therefore was not considered to come under the provisions relating to wife and children. He was not allowed to bring them back under this scheme, and as a matter of fact had considerable difficulty in getting them back under any scheme. It took him a long time and eventually cost him about $1,000. I do not think the act should be interpreted so literally as to exclude a case of that kind, particularly when the man's wife and child had endured some five years of the German occupation. When we come to consider the bill in committee I should like to have an assurance that cases of that kind will be included or that the wording of the act will be changed to include them. This was a case where great injustice was done. I think the man should be reimbursed the amount of money he has paid out to bring his wife and child to this country. The treatment he got was a very bad return for a soldier who spent five years overseas and went through the entire period of fighting1 in northwest Europe.

I want to state, first, that I recognize the problem which was passed to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen). I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) that the immigration branch requires at this time a full-time minister. I do not think immigration can be properly handled by any one person who has to preside over all the ramifications of the Department of Mines and Resources, and if I were advising the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the appointment of a minister of immigration I would recommend

Immigration Act
the hon. gentleman who now occupies the post of Minister of Mines and Resources. I do not think the department could be in more capable or more humane hands. He has also demonstrated, while Speaker of the house, that he is very good at shadow-boxing among the different complexes to be found amongst members on all sides of the house. I believe he is sufficiently well posted in the art of diplomacy to handle this difficult problem of immigration, because it will involve many ramifications in the years to come. Whatever Canada is to be in the future will be determined by the people whom rve bring into this country in the next few years.
I shall be as brief and as explicit in what I have to say as I possibly can. First, I wish to say that I see the question of immigration which confronts Canada today, in two ways. The first and immediate problem which has confronted Canada in the last few years is that of relieving misery in Europe. We were committed to undertake our proportionate share of that relief. Along with all the other countries which were our allies, we went to war for the purpose of liberating the oppressed peoples of Europe who were under nazi domination. Since the armies of liberation went in, about all we have succeeded in doing is impounding these people again. They are still in camps; they are still under military supervision; they are still wondering what is to happen.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced his new regulations a few days ago he said that the immediate concern of the Canadian government was to be that of bringing from Europe refugees and displaced persons who had relatives in this country who were able to provide for them if and when they arrived here. That recommendation must have been written by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), because it is a Scotch recommendation. They are able to come if they can pay their way; if they are not they can stay in the camps in Europe.
Judging from the discussion which has taken place in the house, one would assume that no people were brought to this country during 1946, and that if there were any they were carefully scrutinized on the basis of the announcement of the Prime Minister. That is not true. A few days ago I was surprised when I picked up a copy of the standing committee on immigration and labour's report, dated April 30, 1947. I found that, according to figures tabled by Mr. Jolliffe, deputy minister for immigration, in 1946 we permitted to come to Canada 117,798 people. They were not displaced persons. Of that number, 71,719
came in from the United States, Britain, and so forth. Britain and the United States contributed the largest number. Canadian service personnel dependents to the number of 46,079 came in. That is quite all right. They were legitimately entitled to come, because to all intents and purposes they were Canadians. But the 71,719 who were brought in were not selected on the basis of relieving misery in Europe. They were brought in here apparently because we needed them, not that they needed us.
If the principles announced by the Prime Minister in amending the regulations are to be followed out, then we have to do more than just announce principles. There must be a practical application of them. AVe have taken a lot of people in 1946, but we did not relieve very much misery in Europe. That should have been the first and immediate problem. After the war finished, I believe we should have started immediately and permitted anyone to come into this country who had relatives and friends here who were permitted to assume obligation for them. We have fallen down on the job very badly there.
During the past couple of years our immigration regulations have been restrictive. The reason for that was, of course, the building up of machinery in Europe through which we could work. Nevertheless the practical application of the regulations we may have had has been violated badly, in my opinion, by the government permitting by order in council two industrialists in this country to proceed to Europe and select for their own industries people to come to this country and work. This was done during the time when the house was sitting, during the time when a bill was on the order paper to deal with the question of immigration. During that time an hon. member who operates a textile mill in Quebec was given permission by order in council to proceed to Europe and to select for himself personnel to take employment in his plant. I believe that is something which should be condemned by every right-thinking person in the country. That is commercialized immigration. That will not help relieve the stress among people who are impounded and who have sacrificed everything they had in other countries for the purpose of preserving democracy and freedom in this world. In my opinion, that smacks of the old auction block, of the days of slavery, when the slave was taken onto the market-

That is what I am endeavouring to do, Mr. Speaker. I am talking about immigration; I am talking about backdoor immigration, and I am pointing out to the minister that the regulations, as we have them today, are being violated. I do not expect that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen), with the department he has to supervise today, is able to be in touch with every section of this country and know what is being done by way of immigration. I was pointing out to him that a ship can come in Vancouver, discharge the United States crew, take aboard a Chinese crew or one of any other nationality, and bring them in for that purpose. They do that merely by registering under the Panamanian government. This article, which I need not read- no doubt the minister has read it, since it is in a newspaper from his own province-points out that the merchant marine of both Britain and the United States is being threatened because of racketeers who have registered under the Panamanian government for the purpose of getting around the immigration regulations not only of Canada but also of the United States, by commissioning these ships in that way. So the point I want to make is that this form of backdoor immigration is leaving Canadian seamen on the streets in Vancouver, while these ships are commissioned with aliens under the Panamanian flag. I am just giving that as a piece

Immigration Act

of information to show the minister that his regulations are not being observed as I think he would want them to be.
In regard to the long-range programme of immigration, I agree with the statement made by the Prime Minister, that we can take people into this country only as we are able to absorb them, and that, while we are taking them in, we should be careful to see that the3' fit into the economic structure of Canada. While I am on that subject I would point out to the minister that, before a long-range programme .is undertaken on that basis, there is considerable checking up to be done in Canada. If immigration is to be carried on in this way it must be planned and integrated so that each province will be in a position to absorb its share.
I am going to speak for a moment about my own end of the country. I think it is about time the Canadian government endeavoured to organize the economy of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in such a way as to keep in this country the 15,000 Canadians we have been losing from the mari-times to the United States each year for the past fifteen or twenty years. That statement was made recently in the Nova Scotia legislature; it is not something I am throwing around. If we are to have a long-range immigration programme to bring people into this country, one of the first responsibilities of the government is to check our resources province by province; to develop those resources; to devise some method whereby our own poeple can be placed at work before more people are brought in and dumped into the ranks of the unemployed.
The situation in the maritimes is serious. There is plenty of land there, thousands of vacant farms throughout New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The rehabilitation of those farms is necessary. People in Nova Scotia would go on farms, provided that they could get some assistance. Therefore one of the first obligations of the government in relation to a long-range immigration programme is to check our resources province by province, so that the people who come in will be placed where they may be able to make their best contribution.
In the matter of immigration, Canada is faced with the problem that today we have only two provinces in which there is any industry. The centralization of industry in Ontario and Quebec is one of the things that will retard immigration, and until there is decentralization and the establishment of at least secondary or subsidiary industries both east and west to take up what the basic industries are producing, and immigration

handled accordingly, in such a way as to balance the economy, we shall not get very far with it.

I have listened to this debate for some time with a good deal of interest. I must say I support the statement of the previous speaker in reference to the present government of Great Britain and his criticism of the statement of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey). In one sense, however, they were quite correct, Britain is an occupied country, occupied by an idea whose time has arrived, and which no force can stop.
I was pleased the other day to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announce the government's immigration policy. From now on, in order to answer the many letters I receive in this connection it will not be necessary for me to put together a lot of pieces in order to inform my constituents as to the government's immigration policy. We now have a clear statement, and I am sure that, on the whole, the policy will meet with general acceptance in the house and throughout the country. It was the usual carefully worded, cautious statement, and at the present time I see very little to criticize in connection with it. But I believe it will take a period of time after that policy is put into effect before we can correctly assess it.
Much has been said this evening on this question of immigration, and I am going to be quite brief. Personally, I think our first obligation, as far as immigration is concerned, is to those people, regardless of their nationality, who have suffered because of their opposition to nazism. We must first of all give consideration to admitting those who have demonstrated by their past activities their loyality to democratic principles-and again I say, "regardless of nationality."
Immigration Act
It has always been noticeable to me throughout the years that these racial antagonisms grow when people are at distances from one another, and when they fail to know and understand one another. In the district in which I live there are people of many races: Italian, Polish, German, central Europeans and people of British stock; and these animosities disappear when they get to know one another and work together for some common objective. I have noticed in my experience the wonderful effect of working in cooperative organizations, trade unions and farmer organizations, where they seem to overcome these racial animosities, and build up a spirit of fellowship, by working for a common objective.
Our top priority should be the victims of the nazi concentration and work camps. Before passing on, I wish to urge upon the minister that the many thousands of British veterans who served in this country during the war, and who realize what a great country we have, should not be overlooked. They and their dependents should be brought as soon as possible as immigrants to this country.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said, and correctly, that an immigration policy, to be successful, had to be tied to some planning and development of our natural resources. So far as our immediate immigration policy is concerned, I am all for doing all we can to relieve the suffering of those victims of tyranny in Europe, for bringing them out, possibly to stay with relatives, or to live under temporary conditions until permanently settled.
Then, so far as our long-term policy is concerned, I am quite sure it will not be successful unless it is tied to a planned development of our natural resources. I noticed that one or two speakers in the Progressive Conservative party referred to that, although perhaps they avoided the words "planned1 policy", or avoided the word "planning." I believe, if this policy is to be successful, the government must take into its confidence large representative groups of people. We have to build up in them a spirit of working with a common objective, as we did during the war. We have to give local communities and the larger districts-the provinces, and Canada as a whole- a common objective to work for in the future.
I believe the government should take into its confidence veterans organizations, labour organizations, farmer organizations and employer organizations, and tell them what it is doing from day to day. It should also tell them what it proposes to do, and should seek their advice, thereby so far as possible enmeshing the people of this country in the
Immigration Act

putting into effect of the government's policies. If more of that is done we shall remove in some cases the causes of artificial differences, and give the people something to live for. I am convinced that the more the people are enmeshed in the administration of their own affairs, the better will be the development of this country.
Before concluding, may I say that when the minister speaks I suggest that he give the house more detail on this question of immigration. He should tell us where the government intends to locate immigration officers, the type of staff which will be used in those offices and how it will function, the procedure of selection, the forms to be filled out and the questionnaires used. It should tell us how it intends to make certain that no unsuitable person will enter Canada, the type of medical examination anticipated, and such things as financial standing, and matters of that kind. More than that, I believe that in a matter of immigration, in which all the people of Canada are concerned-and they are concerned in a successful immigration policy and the development of a successful immigration scheme- the government should make a periodical report, not only to the house but to the Canadian people, as to the success they are having in the development of the immigration policy, and in the distribution of these people throughout the country.
In conclusion, I should like to say a few words about the bill under discussion, a bill which, as presented to the house, still permits a measure of discrimination. I am hopeful that when we reach the committee stage the remarks made by various speakers in the debate will cause the minister to consider an amendment to the bill to remove this discrimination. However the bill is a great improvement on the present legislation and, because of that, while still hoping the minister will see fit to amend it, I intend to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish for a few minutes to discuss this measure and, before I shall have finished, I crave your permission to bring one particular case to the attention of the minister.
During this debate we have heard much about doing things without discrimination as to race, colour, creed, sex and so on. These are not new words, nor is the expression a new one. It was adopted in the Atlantic charter by two of the greatest men of this age; it was followed at San Francisco, where the excellent representatives of this country attended. But I could not help wondering, as I sat listening, if all of us who use this expression, and affirm it, have been quite honest in so doing.
(Mr. Herridge.l
Idealism is a wonderful thing. No individual or no nation will get very far unless it holds these ideals high. But that is not the last word, because we live in a practical age. It is easy to say that if we all applied the golden rule to one another we would have no difficulty whatsoever. But unfortunately, sir, two of the most moving factors in human conduct continue to be fear and selfishness. As human beings we are far from perfect in our relationships with one another, or as nation to nation, continent to continent or block to block.
So I come back to this expression, "without discrimination as to race, colour and creed'. It is a wonderful thing to say. It sounds well.
I am not suggesting that anyone in the house has spoken, so to speak, with his tongue in his cheek. We speak about the coloured races and, with respect to them, we say that we want their immigration limited because they will not assimilate.
Let us consider our Jewish friends. I am proud to say that in the place from which I come there are many of them, and among them are some of my most intimate friends. I have discussed this problem with them. They say to me-and truthfully-"You say we are clannish, that we herd together". I say, "Yes, you do". The man I have in mind is an able man, belonging to my own profession, and he says to me, "I want to ask you this question: Why do we do it? The answer is: Because you compel us to do it".
Let us of the white race-and they are of the white race, of course-when we complain about others not being assimilable, admit that it is not the fault of those races. It is our fault that they are not assimilable into our life. I know I am not going to make any friends by what I say now, but I say that those people who rise to heights of oratory and accuse the government or anyone else of discrimination in matters of colour are not honest in doing so unless they are prepared to have their daughters marry these coloured people. That is tough, but it is realistic and it is absolutely
true.	.
I turn now to the question of Chinese immigration, and I wish to say a word for my Chinese friends in the province from which I come. They are splendid citizens. You can go into any small town in Alberta and you will find that the Chinese with the store or restaurant is perhaps the most generous giver to charities, the largest subscriber to victory loans or to any community effort which you will find. In the city in which I live they are highly respected. Look over the crime annals of this country and you will find very few Chinese convicted of serious crimes. Just search your memory and you will find that

Immigration Act
there are few indeed. But I am not suggesting for one moment that, because of that, our doors should be opened wide to large Chinese immigration. I say that, not because of prejudice with respect to race or colour; I say it. because I do not believe it to be in the interest, selfish if you like, of Canadians living in this country. These statements are at least frank and, as I say, they will not do me any good in many places.
I go a step farther. We must stop somewhere. We must admit that what we said in San Francisco means that we shall open our gates wide and lose sovereignty in choosing those people we suggest may come to our shores. We must do one thing or the other. I am still one of those people who, having regard to the interest of this country, think we should be just a little choosy in naming the persons, races if you like, that we ask to come to this country. I do not think this problem is entirely an immigration problem. Take the Chinese, for example. Speaking only for the part of the country where I know them, I know they have succeeded. Why? Because they are prepared to work any number of hours a day in order to get themselves along. My hon. friends over here talk about planning, and I am going to have a word to say about it. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) had something to say about that.

speechtext: I think you will be befojre I have finished, because I will convert you. The hon. member said a moment ago that we in this party had not mentioned the word "planning". Is the budget in this House of Commons anything other than a planning for the future? Are the estimates which we shall soon discuss anything other than planning the country's finances for the coming year? Nothing in this world succeeds without some planning, but the planning that hon. gentlemen to my left want is planning done by their little group to operate the lives of everyone in this country. That form of planning we do not want and I trust we never shall. Now I have dealt with their planning.

speechtext: You did not even come near to it.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I hear a young hon. gentleman over here say that I did not even come near to it. He is half my age, but I will shoot him or I will run him and I will beat him.
To come back to what I was trying to say before I was so agreeably interrupted by my hon. friend to my left, you cannot consider your immigration problem without considering your economic problem. By that I mean hours of work and all that sort of thing. Some people are willing to work long hours, and it is to their credit that they do so in order to benefit themselves in this world. I think you will find that nearly everyone who has succeeded in this world has not paid much attention to an hourly day or an hourly week of some proportion. My hon. friends over here keep saying, "Let us cut the hours shorter and shorter," and at the same time they want to welcome people who are prepared to disregard daily and weekly hours completely. There is a gap there which I should like someone over here to fill in after I have finished.
I agree with the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) and other hon. members on this side who have stated that we are having great difficulty in the operation of our present regulations. In other words, J. think the difficulty is technical. Lest anyone should misunderstand me, may I pay a tribute to Mr. Jolliffe, superintendent of immigration, who has been kindness itself to me and has given every assistance he can. I have been dealing with him in connection with a case, as has the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The facts are comparatively simple and I am going to give names.
There are two people by. the name of Heimers who had lived for a long time in the city from which I come. This married couple worked for Picardy's, which is one of those lunch places that we have, which is owned and controlled in the effete east, which is how you describe Toronto when you want to be polite to them, which I rarely do. I am going to ask the minister to take a note of this case, and I want three ministers to take a note of it because it involves three different departments. These people went to Germany in 1939 to visit the parents of the husband, who lived in a town, the name of which I cannot remember at the moment. With them went a girl by the name of Scotland whose parents I do know very well. She was on her way to Switzerland to study at a university there. Heimers had return tickets both by sea and by rail and were on two months' leave from the positions
Immigration Act

which they held with Picardy's, having saved up their holidays throughout the years. While they were in Germany, war broke out. They endeavoured in every way they could to get home, even consulting the Swiss diplomatic people and seeing everyone with whom they could get in touch. Unfortunately, in one of our bombing raids the Scotland girl, who was not allowed to go to Switzerland, was killed by one of our planes going over Germany.
This man is a naturalized British subject. The wife's parents are naturalized British subjects and live outside Winnipeg. She came with her parents to Canada when a babe three months of age, and she was under the impression that she had been born here. They were arrested -by the gestapo and served a term in gestapo camps. He was beaten and received all the usual treatment that prisoners get in a. gestapo camp. He was there officially because he had sought to leave Germany and had failed to join a troop, the name of which has escaped me for the moment. He escaped from camp just before the Americans came. He escaped with his wife and nurse who helped them to get out, and he met the United States troops. I have copies of letters from United States officers saying that in the skirmish that then took place twenty-four Americans were killed and that, had Heimers not given them information, their casualties would have been numbered in the hundreds.
Somebody has done something with respect to this man that I cannot find out. I have recommendations as to his character from the police in the occupation zone, from United States officers. The reason given that he was not allowed to return was that his wife had not. told the truth as to her citizenship and that she was, in fact, a Russian. She came here a babe in arms at three months of age. Her parents were naturalized and she thought she was too. She travelled on a Canadian passport, which they still keep in shape. While the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I were dealing with Mr. Jolliffe and receiving sympathetic consideration, we suddenly learned that the case was out of his hands. Why? Some other department of government is starting in to cancel this man's naturalization, and it has been cancelled, although lie has not even been heard. He is told now that he can go to Berlin.-I think it is Berlin-about the end of July and make his appeal. [DOT]
I am not talking about people of whom I do not know something; although I do not know them personally, I know a great many of their friends. This man worked and organized one of those displaced persons camps for the Americans from May until July, resigned

his job and started to go home. He cannot get to England. We are worrying about bringing people in from here and there. Let me in fairness say this. There may be something in this case which I do not know. The reason I do not know it is not because I have not tried to find out.
There we find these two people, Canadians if there ever were Canadians, imprisoned by the gestapo on account of a lack of sympathy with the nazi cause, and we cannot get them home. The man's naturalization is cancelled wilhout his even being heard. With great respect, I want to know how this government or any agency of this government can cancel this man's naturalization without giving him an opportunity to be heard. An appeal at some indefinite time and at some indefinite place is just not good enough. I leave that.
I have not mentioned it in this house, although we have been here for two and a half months, but in conversation with my hon. friend, the member for Winnipeg North Centre, we thought perhaps it was time that it was brought to the minister's attention. Let me again repeat that I have received no discourtesy whatever from the department, noth- [DOT] ing but- kindness and generosity in Mr. Jolliffe's treatment of me and, I am sure, of my hon. friend as well.
I now turn to the broad policy of immigration and I shall be only a moment or two. We heard the policy announced the other day and1 everyone has been loud in his praise of it,
I am sure I would join that happy and cheering throng if I knew exactly what it meant.
I can understand the short-range plan because that is simple. We are simply enlarging the field of relatives allowed1 in. We are all for that. I am quite sure that no one will deny that.
But what is this great long-range policy that we have heard of? I know it covers pages; but here is what it is in a sentence: We shall take what the country can absorb. That is it in one sentence. There is just nothing more to it. With that I am in hearty agreement. But- and here is where my planner friend, the hon. member for Kootenay West, might even agree with me, I think we should have something more than the mere statement, with which we will all agree, that we shall take as many as the absorptive capacity of the country can take. What is the absorptive capacity of the country? Is it one thousand, two thousand, ten thousand, one hundred' thousand, two hundred thousand a year? I have not the least idea what it means and perhaps the minister would go into more detail when he closes the debate. I sincerely trust that he will, because no one will dispute that this country should have all the immigration that

Immigration Act
its absorptive capacity will permit-and that, we are told by people on both sides of the house, is an immigration policy showing great vision! It is just a trite phrase, a truism. It is meaningless, unless we learn from the minister who operates this department just what that means in numbers and in the type of persons that we are to absorb.
I want to point out-and in saying this I appreciate the difficulties of the minister and of the government at this time-that the last large immigration we had was back in the 1900's. I knew something about that, because I worked on a railroad widening dump on an extra gang with a lot of people who had come in at that time. But in those days we had free homesteads and our immigration came largely to settle on free land. Instead of people reading figures to me out of books and telling me how many millions of acres of arable land we have in western Canada, I want somebody to tell me where they are. I want somebody to tell me how close they are to a railway. I want somebody to tell me how much brush and rock there are on them. We are not living today back in the 19O0's. We have an entirely different situation to meet, and it seems to me that the immigration which we now seek must go largely into industry in this country. This confronts us with an entirely different problem from that which we met back in the 1900's.
Therefore may I close by saying that I am glad the Chinese Exclusion Act is being repealed. I thoroughly believe that at some day this house must admit that the problem of British Columbia with respect to orientals is not a provincial matter but a dominion matter, in the same way that I say, with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia has ceased to be a provincial matter and is something which must be regarded as for the benefit of the whole country.

The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and I do not always see eye to eye; but, as he has already indicated, it was by agreement between the two of us that we decided to raise this afternoon or this evening the case to which he has already made reference. He has given the particulars in considerable detail and little more needs to be added; but I would join with him in urging the minister, either through his own department or by whatever necessary contact needs to be made with two other departments, to try to have this case settled as quickly as possible.
If he looks up the record he may find one -slight discrepancy in the account which was
given by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I set it right so that the minister will not be able to tell my friend that he was wrong. It has to do with the status of Mrs. Heimers who did become a Canadian by the naturalization of her parents and who was a Canadian until she married. At the time she married, her husband had not yet been naturalized. He was naturalized later, but that naturalization did not cover her. She did not know that when she went to Germany. I emphasize the point, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has already done, that these people, possessing the German language, Mr. Heimers being of German descent, endured a great deal of persecution, as one can imagine, because of their refusal to cooperate with the German authorities while they were in that country during the war.
It does seem to me that the appeal which the hon. member has made and which I support, should receive thorough consideration in the hope that action might be taken at an early date. As he has indicated, our contacts have been with three departments, the Department of Immigration, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of the Secretary of State. I hold in my hand a letter which I received a few days ago from the acting under-secretary of state for external affairs, dated April 25, referring to this case and saying in part;
Mr. Heimers requested that his case be heard by a commission of inquiry.
The letter explains that a formal notice that his naturalization was to be revoked had been served on Mr. Heimers. I quote further:
This request was granted, but the office of the registrar of Canadian citizenship advised by telephone today that the case would not be heard until August, 1947, which is the next sitting of the commission.
In the meantime, according to letters which I have received from members of the family here in Canada, Mr. and Mrs. Heimers have been moved from one camp to another, and their plight is really as pitiable as that of any of the displaced persons about whom so much has been rightly said during the course of this debate. These people, however, are Canadians, simply away from home.
I might explain that my connection with the case arises from the fact that Mrs. Heimers has a sister in Winnipeg whom I know, and they have two brothers who served in the Canadian forces during the war, one in the army and one in the air force. All these things together make it seem a pretty pitiable case, and I do hope that the action which my hon. friend and I have taken in raising this
Immigration Act

matter in the house after so many months of contact with the departments concerned will result, in effect, in consideration being given to it at an early day.
While I am on my feet, I just want to add my voice to the expressions that have been given with regard to the progress we are making in eliminating racial discrimination from our statute books. I use that word advisedly. We are making progress. But the point that some of us have been trying to make is that the government will not get in the eyes of the world, if you like, the credit that it deserves for such steps as it has taken until it goes at least one little step farther. As the minister knows, until recently there were on the statute books of Canada three measures effecting discrimination against the Chinese. There was, first of all, the Chinese Immigration Act. Then there was the order in council denying to Chinese in Canada the right to become naturalized unless they got the permission of their government. Then there is order in council P.C. 2115. Of these three measures, two are now to go by the board. The bill before us, when it becomes law, will repeal the Chinese Immigration Act, and the other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced the revocation of the order in council respecting naturalization. But that leaves upon the statute books of Canada order in council P.C. 2115, which still discriminates against people of Canada on racial lines.
I hold in my hand a copy of today's Toronto Globe and Mail. One perhaps should be quoting from the Winnipeg Free Press when he is addressing the government. Their pages are full of advice along these lines, but I quote this because it is current. The Globe and Mail takes the position that the government should surely go one step farther and give to all persons residing in Canada the same rights or impose against them the same restrictions without drawing a racial line. I quote the significant sentence from the Globe and Mail editorial:
There should be no restrictions on human beings of any race or national origin living in Canada which do not apply ,with equal weight and effectivness to all.
I hope that when the minister replies in this debate he will tell us whether any consideration is being given to the repeal of P.C. 2115.

speechtext:
I wish to say a few words on this immigration bill. I come from a riding which, during the last war, sent as many men per capita as any rural riding in the Dominion of Canada. There are many families in my riding who sent four boys, and that is a record to be proud of. The population of my riding is mostly British, although some are Polish, Ukrainian, Swedish, Norwegian and German; and I must say that out of this great melting-pot they have emerged as true Canadians.
Last spring I had the pleasure of attending a reception in one township largely populated' by Mennonites, and I was struck by the loyalty of these boys and the number enlisted as they came forward to receive their gifts presented by the township in appreciation of their sacrifices for Canada. I remember well speaking to one of these settlers; he was the father

Immigration Act
of one of these boys. He told me that his father stole out of Germany at the age of seventeen, came to Canada, took up a bush lot, and out of the forest hewed a home for himself and his family. That these people have contributed much to our country, cannot be disputed. One needs only to drive through this district to see the fine barns and houses which have been erected.
I would ask the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) if offices where prospective immigrants may apply will be set up in England, Scotland and Ireland as well as in other countries mentioned. In this connection we should not forget that the Norwegians, the Swedes and the Danes blend well with our people. True, we must help with the displaced people of Europe, but we must see to it that we are not bringing to our shores those who are communistic in any way. That is the real danger. I am sure that the government will guard against this. We must build in Canada a nation of truly democratic people so that we may become a great nation. We have plenty of room and many vacant farms. I think an immigration policy along selective lines is the one for Canada. We want more people to use our products, to work in the factories and on the farms.
