speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say, in
the first instance, that I think this debate on immigration has been really worth while. I am indeed glad to have the expression of opinion which has been given from all sides of the house with regard to it. To me, the one surprising thing was the unanimity, the agreement that there was about the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on May 1. That statement was, of course, the result of constant and close attention given to the many problems arising. It was felt-and I think all will agree-that it should come with the authority of the Prime Minister, and he made the statement for the government.
When opening the debate on this bill I did not speak at any great length, because I was of the opinion then, as I am now, that when I was dealing with a bill of this kind my duty was to confine myself to the terms of the bill, and that a general discussion of immigration on that bill was entirely out of order; and I expressed myself to that effect. But during the course of the debate it has broadened out, and has become a debate on immigration in general. Therefore I shall have to reply
to many of the things which have been said, hoping that when we come to the bill we shall be able to confine ourselves to it.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) was critical of my attitude in that respect. But I think he will agree with me that the attitude I took then was the proper one in the circumstances with regard to a bill such as this. I said then that the effects of the bill and the provisions of it I would be able to deal with in committee when we got to it; and I hope I shall be able now to deal with the criticism and the suggestions that have been made by hon. members, and do so within the time limit this time, although I may have to ask the consent of the house to extend it.
First of all, I would point out that when hon. members are talking about policy with regard to immigration, sometimes that term is loosely used, and what they are really asking for are amendments to the regulations under which our immigration policy is carried out. For the purposes of the record I think I should state now just the steps which have been taken with regard to immigration. From 1930 on, as everyone knows, there has been very little immigration. In that year, 1930, the Bennett government passed order in council P.C. 2115. That is the one which has been discussed a great deal by hon. gentlemen of the C.C.F. party. That order provides as follows:
From and after the 16th August, 1930, until otherwise ordered, the landing in Canada of any immigrant of any Asiatic race is hereby prohibited except as hereinafter provided:
The immigration officer in charge may admit any immigrant who otherwise complies with the provisions of the Immigration Act, if it is shown to his satisfaction that such immigrant is-
The wife or unmarried child under eighteen years of age of any Canadian citizen legally admitted to and resident in Canada, who is in a position to receive and care for his dependents. Provided-
And this proviso is the one that is a matter of concern at this moment.
-that this regulation shall not apply to the nationals of any country in regard to which there is in operation a law, a special treaty, or agreement, or convention regulating immigration.
This order in council contained a proviso, as will be noted, which made it not applicable to persons of Chinese race, their admission being governed by the Chinese Immigration Act which we now have before us.
On March 21, 1931, the Bennett government passed order in council P.C. 695, which set forth the provisions under which immigrants may land in Canada and which drastically reduced immigration into the country. Certain amendments have been made by the present
Immigration Act

government. The consequence of the passing of P.C. 695 and P.C. 2115 was to diminish immigration to a trickle, and the machinery for immigration was greatly reduced. When the war came in 1939, naturally all immigration from the continent of Europe ceased. The position in Europe today, two years after the war, is still chaotic. Travel is difficult and, in many cases, impossible. Frontier difficulties are extremely great, and the immigration authorities have found great difficulty in reestablishing their inspectional facilities on the continent.
The first duty of the government was to arrange for the return of service men and their dependents. This was accomplished in a shorter period than was ever contemplated, and the government was immediately faced with requests for the entrance of many people resident in Europe who had relatives in this country. Nine months after the finish of hostilities, the government widened the door to permit the entry of certain classes of relatives of these residents of Canada. The government believed that it could give relief to the anxieties of many of our residents and citizens by permitting the entry of their relatives, and that these should have a priority for entry from abroad. Further, these new immigrants could be accommodated with their relatives, and thus would not render more difficult the extreme shortage of housing, because at that time the housing problem was acute. Therefore order in council P.C. 2071 was passed on May 28, 1946, adding to the classes of immigrants who might enter Canada:
The father or mother, the unmarried son or daughter eighteen years of age or over, the unmarried brother or sister, the orphan nephew or niece under sixteen years of age, of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada who is in a position to receive and care for such relatives.
The term "orphan" used in this clause means a child 'bereaved of both parents.
Since that date, following representations made by many people in Canada and after investigation by officials, the government decided to enlarge the provisions of the regulations with regard to the admissible classes of relatives and also to include and provide for the admission of other categories of occupational groups whose entry was desirable. Accordingly on 30th January of this year P.C. 371 was passed, providing for the admission of the wife, unmarried son, daughter, brother or sister, father or mother, widowed daughter or sister with or without unmarried children under eighteen years of age, orphan nephew' or niece under eighteen years of age, of any person legally admitted to and resident in Canada who is in a position to receive

and care for such relatives. The term "orphan" used in this clause means a child bereaved of both parents.
This order in council further provided for the admission of (a) an agriculturist having sufficient means to farm in Canada; (b) an agriculturist entering Canada to farm, when destined to a father, father-in-law, son, son-in-law, brother, brother-in-law, uncle or nephew engaged in agriculture as his principal occupation, who is in a position to receive such immigrant and establish him on a farm; (c) a farm labourer entering Canada to engage in assured farm employment; and (d) a person experienced in mining, lumbering or logging, entering Canada to engage in assured employment in any one of such industries. The last order in council was presented by the Prime Minister when he made his statement the other day. It substitutes paragraph 3 and makes the following as the regulations under which immigration will be coming to Canada. It provides for the husband or wife, the son, the daughter, the brother or sister together with husband or wife and unmarried children, if any; the father or mother, the orphan nephew or niece under twenty-one years of age of any person legally resident in Canada who is in a position to receive and care for such relatives. The term "orphan" used in this clause means a child bereaved of both parents; and 5: a person entering Canada for the purpose of marriage to a legal resident thereof, provided that the prospective husband is able to maintain his intended wife.
In order to cope with what undoubtedly would be greatly increased immigration, it was recognized that steps had to be taken immediately to set up inspectional services in Europe. This was no easy matter. Suitable accommodation had to be obtained, and what would have been simple in pre-war days became a major problem in war-ravaged Europe. There were further delays in the necessary negotiations with the different governments in the countries where these inspectional facilities had to be set up, but by the end of 1946 those facilities were established in France, Belgium and Holland, and facilities for examination were established by Canadian missions in Norway, Denmark, Greece and Portugal. Also facilities are now available for Switzerland and Czechoslovakia, and it is expected that arrangements will be made for Poland shortly. With every possible dispatch the department is completing the administrative details to cope with the large immigration created by these wider and amended regulations.

Immigration Act
I was much interested in listening Friday evening to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) give an account of his recent experiences in Europe. The hon. gentleman probably left Germany before our inspectional teams went into that country, and the other evening he asked what arrangements if any had been made by this government with regard to refugees in that country. Prior to the war, under its mandate the IGCR dealt *with persons who fled from their country of residence or citizenship before the second world war for reasons of race, religion, nationality or political oppression. During the second world war the mandate was extended to include additional displaced persons; persons who, as a result of the action of the nazi or fascist regimes, were deported from or obliged to leave their country of nationality or former residence for forced labour or other causes; persons who have resided in Germany or Austria, being of Jewish origin, or foreigners or stateless persons victims of nazi persecution. The mandate does not include nationals of enemy countries, volkdeutsche, prisoners of war in allied hands, war criminals, traitors, persons who have assisted enemy forces, and those who fled into Germany to avoid falling into allied hands.
The hon. gentleman asked, why not set up immigration offices in Germany, Austria and Italy? There would be no advantage in setting up. regular immigration inspectional offices in those countries at this time, because prospective immigrants could not proceed to such points of examination. Those enemy countries are under military control, and residents cannot move freely from place to place. The department now has two inspectional teams in Germany examining displaced persons whose cases have been approved. The intergovernmental committee on refugees locates these prospective immigrants, obtains travel permits, et cetera, and transfers them to convenient centres for examination by the examination teams. These teams will also operate in Austria, and possibly in Italy in the same way.
On Friday the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) made reference to persons of German ethnic origin, but who are not German nationals, who are now in occupied territory. It is quite true that the IGCR is not empowered to deal with these people. The Canadian government, however, is prepared to accept as immigrants those of this category who are otherwise qualified for admission to our country. Canadian immigration officers have been directed to facilitate their entry. It is. of course, difficult under
present circumstances to take effective action. We are, however, doing what we can to solve this problem.

The hon. member suggested that P.C. 2115 is not enough, and that it could be repealed. That is true; it could be repealed, but I would refer the hon. gentleman to the statement made by the Prime Minister, in which at page 2646 of Hansard he said:
I wish to state quite definitely that, apart from the repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act and the revocation of order in council P.C. 1378 of June 17, 1931, regarding naturalization, the government has no intention of removing the existing regulations respecting Asiatic immigration unless and until alternative measures of effective control have been worked out. Canada recognizes the right of all persons seeking to become permanent residents. We claim precisely the same right for our country.
I think that answers that question.
The other question the hon. member asked was, "I would like to ask the Prime Minister what has happened to that treaty"-meaning the Chinese immigration treaty-"and why has the treaty not been concluded. Is the matter still open, and is it intended to conclude such a treaty?"
The answer is that up to the present it has not been found possible to reach agreement on the basis of a treaty that would be satisfactory to both countries. The matter is still open for further negotiation. And I think the sentence I have already read with regard to the Canadian government's being prepared at any time to enter into negotiations with these countries for special agreements for the control and admission of immigrants on a basis of complete equality and reciprocity answers that question.
The other question the hon. gentleman asked was, "Does the present order in council, in the light of the Prime Minister's statement yesterday, mean that all the wives and families of those Canadian Chinese now resident in Canada shall be permitted to come to Canada

when this bill is repealed and the order in council is in force as the only means of governing Chinese immigration?"
The answer to that is that the wives, and the children under 18 years of age, of Canadian citizens, can come to Canada.
Then the hon. gentleman asked another question regarding the influx of these numbers and what it would mean, and whether they would all be in this year. I will reply to that later.
I should like now to deal with the question of what it has meant in the way of extension of the regulations by way of immigration. I take it that these regulations will probably be sufficient to cover more immigrants than those for whom there is transportation available.

I should like to address myself to the remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell) and those made today by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). When the bill was first introduced on February 11 the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar used pretty strong language in referring to what he termed1 "hoax" and "hypocrisy". As reported on page 331 of Hansard, he asked that P.C. 2115 be repealed and that citizens, regardless of race or creed
or colour, be placed on the same footing in this country. After reading a press statement, he went on to say:
What do we find upon examination of this measure? That discrimination is to remain unless, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggested this afternoon, we bring all our immigration under order in council P.C. 2115 instead of order in council P.C. 695. Because if we fail to remove this limited Chinese immigration from P.C. 2115 and bring it under P.C. 695, what have we? We have renewed discrimination:	That a resident in Canada of
Chinese origin must be a Canadian citizen before he can bring his wife and family into this country, whereas a Canadian resident of European origin can bring his wife and his children under eighteen years of age into this country, whether he is a citizen or not. To remove discrimination we must make the choice.
Well, now, what does that mean? P.C. 2115 was passed on September 16, 1930, by the Bennett government for the purpose of dealing with the entry of Asiatics into this country. That order, which I have already read, provided that the regulations should not apply to the nationals of any country in regard to which there was in operation a law or special treaty or agreement or convention regarding immigration. Such a law now exists with regard to the Chinese and will continue to exist until the house repeals the Chinese Immigration Act by Bill No. 10, which we are now discussing.
By repealing P.C. 2115 the hon. member has proposed to remove discrimination between Europeans and Asiatics and to place that Asiatic immigration under the provisions contained in P.C. 695. That has been emphasized this afternoon by both the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Mackenzie. His last sentence in the paragraph I have read, reads, "To remove discrimination we must make the choice." Supposing we made that choice and removed the discrimination to which the hon. member refers. All Asiatics would1 then be entitled to apply to be admitted as immigrants who could comply with the provisions of P.C. 695. Take one category only-and others are equally applicable to Asiatics-that of a farm labourer entering Canada to engage in assured farm employment, as an example. Would any one doubt that many thousands of Chinese could qualify as such?
The house will recall that I asked both the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Mackenzie if their argument was to repeal P.C. 2115, leave all immigration under P.C. 695 and delete from P.C. 695 the clause which provides that the provisions of the order in council shall not apply to immigrants of any Asiatic race. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not

He said, to remove discrimination we must make the choice; that is, the government must make the choice. I suggest to these hon. gentlemen that to remove discrimination they must make the choice as to whether they will include Asiatics in P.C. 695 and grant them all the privileges now enjoyed by European immigrants or, conversely, to remove that discrimination between these people and take from the Europeans, the Ukrainians, the Poles and all those from continental Europe the privileges which they have enjoyed for so many years under the law. The government would have to repeal the provisions concerning Asiatics as contained in P.C. 695.
These extensions, or widening of the doors as some call it, were made because of widespread opinion throughout the country that we should take some steps to assist people in Europe who were relatives of residents and citizens of Canada. The repeal of that order would not, I think, meet with very much approval. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar gave as his opinion on February 11 what I have quoted, but shortly thereafter he had somewhat of a change of mind. His oratorical outburst brought doubts and the apostolic certainty with which he then spoke required modification. In any event, the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday evening, February lo, reported an interview which he had given md in which he is reported to have said:
In conformity with the united nations charter .here should be equality of treatment for all foreigners under Canadian immigration law.
Further on, he is reported to have said: However, equality of treatment as to admission to Canada having been established by law, he favoured "gentlemen's agreements" being made with India and China on a reciprocal basis to govern the numbers of East Indians and Chinese to be admitted to the dominion. 
In a further paragraph it is stated:
Mr. Coldwell agreed that the acid test of assimilability is intermarriage but, he added, neither the Chinese nor the Indian governments favour intermarriage of their nationals coming to Canada.

Yes, they were in agreement with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I was pointing out that the repeal of P.C. 2115 meant that all the regulations with regard to immigration would come under P.C. 695, and that the deletion of the sentence at the end referring to Asiatics would give Asiatics the same right of entry into our country as Europeans obtained under the law. I pointed out that that would be the effect of the policy advocated by the hon. gentleman, and that, conversely, if he did not want that, he would have to remove the discrimination between Asiatics and Europeans by denying to Europeans the rights they have hitherto had under the law to obtain entry into Canada and bring in their wives and children.
The hon. gentleman asked the government to take its choice. The government is taking its choice. The choice is being taken by asking the house to repeal the Chinese Immigration Act, and the control will then be placed under P.C. 2115.
As to the admittance of Chinese residents in Canada to the privileges of citizenship, the impediment, which was almost insuperable, has been removed by rescinding the order in council requiring them to have the consent of the minister of the interior. The government

Immigration Act
has made its choice and it is in conformity with the policy stated by' the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the house on May 1, at page 2646 of Hansard, where he said:
I wish to state quite definitely that, apart from the repeal of the Chinese Immigration Act and the revocation of order in council P.C. 1378 of June 17, 1931, regarding naturalization, the government has no intention of removing the existing regulations respecting Asiatic immigration unless and until alternative measures of effective control have been worked out. Canada recognizes the right of all other countries to control the entry or non-entry of persons seeking to become permanent residents. We claim precisely the same right for our country.
I wish to make it equally clear that the Canadian government is prepared, at any time, to enter into negotiations with other countries for special agreements for the control of admission of immigrants on a basis of complete equality and reciprocity.
The government has made its position clear.
The hon. gentleman also expressed grave anxiety and concern about Canada's position in the united nations if we did not accede to his wishes. I would be much more concerned and feel much more anxiety if this bill did not pass, because then it could be said with justice -and in my judgment the accusation would be unanswerable-that by refusing to give Canadian citizens of Chinese origin the right to have their wives and children live with them in Canada we had violated the charter and denied those citizens what has been and should be considered as an inalienable right to live in family. We say, further, that legal residents in Canada of Chinese origin may become citizens and have the right to bring their wives and children under eighteen years of age, and in order that no obstacle shall be placed in the way of doing that, P.C. 1378 has been repealed. This government has gone much farther than any preceding government. By the bill before us we are removing any hindrance to Chinese residents in Canada from becoming naturalized citizens. That is the policy which the Prime Minister enunciated in his statement of May 1, and that is what, I repeat, is being carried out.
The question was raised, and an endeavour made to make it a debating point, that Australia had made arrangements with the British government by which Australia was able to secure immigrants in much larger numbers than Canada was ever able to do. I would refer hon. members to the statement made in the House of Lords at Westminster by Lord* Addison in column 1064 of the British Hansard. He was dealing with the question of how many emigrants the British government could deal with and said the 'numbers would be very much fewer than the number of applicants. He went on to say that the number moved in the first year would probably be
6,000	to 6,900, or something like that, and that the numbers would be more than doubled the next year. I mention that to show the house that the difficulty in obtaining transportation is very great. We are continually in communication with the high commissioner in London. WTe have explored and shall continue to explore and exhaust every avenue by which we may get ships to bring in the immigrants who are ready to come to our country in larger numbers.
In closing, let me say, so far as the anxiety of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is concerned about our position before the united nations, I am quite sure that the representatives of this government in the person of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) will so conduct themselves that the interests of Canada will not be prejudiced.

The purpose of the proposed amendment to section 33 of the Immigration Act is to give authority to the immigration inspector in charge at a port of entry to safeguard the passing in direct transit through Canada from one port to another of groups of persons who, not being admissible as immigrants, might remain in Canada if not so controlled. The proposed amendment will enable the inspector in charge at the port of entry to ensure the departure of such parties by requiring the transportation company carrying them across Canada to place a bond as a guarantee of departure. Paragraph 16 will authorize the governor general in council to prescribe the amount and form of the bonds and make regulations for the guarding of such persons while in transit and for their detention at the port of exit while waiting embarkation or completion of arrangements for their departure.
It often happens that bodies of men come from one port and go across Canada to the south. In order that we might have some control of these men, it is thought necessary to have this provision so that we shall know who the parties are that are going across the country.

I wish to correct a misunderstanding that has arisen with regard to my
Immigration Act

speech on the matter of immigration. I spoke on the second reading of the bill on February 11. Outside of about five minutes that I took on Monday, April 28, to speak on the motion to go into supply, I have not had anything to say regarding the merits of the bill. For many years past I have been a consistent supporter of the Polish people. Today the Minister of Labour complained about misleading headlines in the Montreal Standard of Sunday last with regard to Polish soldiers. I wish to complain about the same thing. With regard to the Toronto newspaper I have in mind, especially the heading of April 29 last, I have not a complaint; it is just a difference of opinion.
In the return which the Minister of Labour gave to me he distinctly said that some of the Poles were conscripted into the German army, but that they fought on the Italian front and in northwest Europe. In addition to that, the minister of labour in the old1 country, Mr. Isaacs, reported to the British house that
58,000	of these men were in uniform in the military camps in Britain since the German war closed. They are not doing anything at all with the exception of 400 who are working on the farms and some in the woods. If we wish to bring them here, let us have some of these men, instead of those from Italy, because there were 1,902 Polish airmen killed in the battle of Britain. If there are to be priorities these are the Polish men who should be brought here instead of some of the others. There is a difference of opinion as to whether some of them or all enlisted voluntarily or were conscripted. There is a big difference of opinion on that; a difference in England, Italy, Canada, and a difference in the United States; so much so that Mr. Byrnes, who was secretary of state in the United States, refused to permit them to come to the United States.
I have always been, between the two wars and in them, a supporter of the Polish people. Before the second war I urged that we should lend them money, after Munich, to secure an airport. In conclusion, I wish to say that there should1 be a further check-up or report so that the Canadian people will know how many were volunteers and how many are not. The matter should be cleared up, because there are five or six different opinions on it. Looking through, the British, Canadian and United States press, the British Hansard, the library, and reading Mr. Byrnes' statement and the statement of the minister of labour of Great Britain, Mr. Isaacs, and the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Immigration here who made a clear statement-he generally does 
make a clear statement on any matter that he discusses-I find that there is a difference of opinion on this matter.
I have no objection to the bill. As I said at the beginning, I made a statement when the bill came up on February 11. Between the two wars a million men went away to the United States by emigration. With regard to priorities, it should be given to the British people.
My third reference is to shipping. There is not a ship today for British people to come to this country. On February 11, I urged that they should have priority; that we should utilize the merchant marine and all kinds of vessels to bring them here. During the war we borrowed many ships from the French, the United States and the British. If there is to be any priority at all, I have always contended that it should be shown to our own kith and kin in the old country before we open the doors wide to European-wide immigration, and provide emergency ships for them.

Just before the section passes, I wish to say a few words. I have no particular objection to the section passing, but I believe it is fitting that the members of the committee should realize what we are doing in passing this bill. The figures which the minister gave, if I remember correctly, indicate that there are just about as many Chinese in British Columbia as there are in all the rest of Canada put together. In passing this law we are simply saying to British Columbia, "We are going to dump an impossible problem on your doorstep; you must take it and like it". We in the other parts of Canada, many of the provinces of which have an almost negligible number of Chinese living in them, are telling British Columbia what she must take. I hope that, in the working out of the policy, the government and the minister will take some sort of measure to see that some sort of justice is given to British Columbia. If that is not done I believe the members of this house will live to rue the day. You cannot expect a province of British people to take a monstrous injustice, such as is being forced upon them in this bill, and tamely submit to it. I think we must face that fact.
All the time while the Japanese were going into British Columbia, the men in charge at Ottawa callously and short-sightedly disregarded- the interests of British Columbia. What was the result? Something we are all sorry about today. We disregarded British Columbia, because all she could send here was about seventeen or eighteen members. Such a few members can talk themselves black in the face and the members from other parts of Canada can shrug indifferent shoulders and disregard their pleadings. In my judgment, that is not the kind of attitude upon which to build a strong, united and secure Canada.
There is another matter that comes to my mind. I do not wish to say anything to occasion undue alarm, but a good many members of the house would appear to be taking the point of view that we are never going to face any further difficulty with people from the orient, and that the last war has been fought with people from the orient. I do not think people in our generation have a right to take that supine attitude. We have in our keeping the welfare of generations yet unborn.

Immigration Act
Once more I urge that, in working out this bill and in the administration of the policy, the minister and the government take pains to see that there is not an impossible accumulation of people of the oriental races in the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I wish to say at once that I deeply appreciate the solicitude of the hon. member for Lethbridge for British Columbia; but I want to tell him that as long as that province continues to send to this house such alert and vigilant representatives, in every party, as have been sent to this parliament, British Columbia has nothing to fear for the future.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: This section has to do with the Chinese, and I, too, should like to express to the hon. member for Lethbridge my appreciation, on behalf of the people of British Columbia, for his remarks this evening. We are always grateful for help of this type, and we have had it all too seldom here in years gone by. I should like to check with the minister the figures he gave a few minutes ago in the course of his speech, concerning the number of Chinese who might be able to bring in their wives and children under the new government policy. In the first place, I would ask whether those figures are of the present wives of Chinese, or whether they take into account future marriages.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: They are the present wives.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I understand, then, that the figures the minister gave deal only with Chinese already married?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: The figures are from the census of 1941, giving the total population.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I understood the minister to say there were 8,749 Chinese born in Canada or naturalized here. Was that figure correct? That was the figure the minister gave on February 11.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: And of that number, the minister said it was estimated there were 6,547 married Chinese who could take advantage of this change in the law.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
There were 6,694 persons of
the Chinese race born in Canada.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am getting at the minister's estimate of the number in that group of 8,749 who could take advantage of the change in the law and bring their wives from China. The figure I have is 6,547.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
The number of persons of the Chinese race eligible to bring wives and children to Canada would be approximately
6.547.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Then the minister said there were approximately 26,000 Chinese who are not Canadian citizens?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Then the minister estimated that about one-third of those might take advantage of the new provision?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That was a guess, an approximation.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
That would be about 8,666. As I understand it, from the figure of 6,547 the minister deducted 3,000 who, he said, probably would not take advantage of the provision. For example, he said about 2,000 young Chinese males in Canada would probably marry young Chinese females in Canada, and there were certain other exceptions, making a total of 3,000 which he deducted from the
6.547,	leaving 3,547 who might take advantage of the provision.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Add to that figure the 8,666 and we get a total of 12,213. So the estimate of the government is that 12,213 Chinese males, married at this time, may well take advantage of this provision and bring in their wives and children under eighteen years of age. Is that correct?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes, that is substantially correct. Of course the assumption would be that they would become naturalized.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes, the 8,666 would first have to become naturalized. In addition to that, as I understood it, any Chinese who is a Canadian citizen can go to China, get married and bring back his wife, though under our new citizenship law she is not a Canadian citizen. Is that correct?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: There is no doubt about it; they can go to China, get married and bring their wives back to Canada?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes. I would not want to limit the boundaries of love for a Chinese citizen of this country who wished to go abroad and marry someone in another country. I do not think I would care to be one of those to object.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I am very glad the minister is such an ally- and supporter of Cupid. I just want to get the figures. The position
Immigration Act

then, is that, according to the government's own estimate, we face a possible influx of 12,213 Chinese wives, and, in addition, whatever children are under eighteen years of age. In addition, from now on we can have Chinese go to the orient, marry and bring back their wives?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That will be the situation when the act is repealed.	[DOT]

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is the position we face at the present time?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Today about fifty-three per cent of all the Chinese in Canada are in British Columbia, so that British Columbia would have to face the prospect of having well over half those wives and children settling in that province. The minister will admit that is a reasonable estimate ?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: It is purely an estimate.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Well, may I suggest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and other members from British Columbia, apart from the C.C.F. members who in the last few days in this house have spared no effort to get orientals for British Columbia, that this may very well be a serious situation, and that it may call for some change in government policy or for some amendment to P.C. 2115 when we can see just how the order in council works out. On the basis of the very estimate given by the Minister of Mines and Resources, there is the possibility of an influx into Canada of Chinese wives and children which may be as great as the total Chinese population in Canada at the present time, which is 34,627.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Would the hon. member deny a husband, by law, the right to live with his wife?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Then, can the minister tell us the present law in the United States? As I understand it, when they repealed their Chinese Exclusion Act they put the Chinese on a quota.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I have here the reports from the United States congress, showing that the quota is 105 a year, allowed to come into the United States. There is some provision made in addition to that for the Chinese wives of United States citizens. That was passed in August, 1946.
I have been unable to get complete information with regard to the provision respecting the entry of wives. But, through the parlia-
'Mr. Gresn.]	'
mentary library, did get a report from the Chinese embassy to the effedt that the quota allowed is twenty-five Chinese wives who may be allowed to enter the United States; but, that in fact, since the change in the law only about ten had come into that country.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That twenty-five is allowed how frequently?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: The answer from the librarian stated that the quota allowed twenty-five Chinese wives to enter the United States-and I presume that is each year-but that, in fact, only about ten had come into the country since then. I am not sure that these figures are accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I do no't think they are.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Could the minister give us a full statement of the present United States law?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I have not that.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I would suggest that he get those figures, because it would seem there is quite a big difference between the United States law and the proposed Canadian law. That should be checked by the minister's department. I understand that at the present time he has no figures under the United States law.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: My information-and probably it was entirely incorrect-was that the United States law was much more generous than we are trying to be in this instance.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: No; I think the minister will find that that is not so. Certainly the quota now for Chinese into the United States is 105 a year. There may be wives of United States citizens allowed over and above that. I would ask the minister to get those figures.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver South said a few minutes ago that members of the C.C.F. group in the house- and I use the words he used-had spared no effort to get orientals for British Columbia in the last few days. That statement is so obviously inaccurate that I cannot but rise to comment upon it. We are not anxious to secure orientals for British Columbia.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: You certainly do not talk that way.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
Nor are we anxious in that respect for any part of Canada. But we are anxious to see to it that a country which calls itself democratic shall remove the last

Immigration Act
vestiges of racial discrimination. That is the point. And so far as immigration of orientals into this country goes, there are few orientals who want to come to this country, a country in which they have never been particularly welcome. I say again to the minister, as I said on February 11, I think it was, that if this country were prepared to enter into a gentlemen's agreement with the Chinese government, the flow of Chinese immigrants into this country could be controlled.
But we are not discussing Chinese immigration in this bill. What we are discussing, actually, is the right of a Chinese to bring into this country his wife and his children under eighteen years of age. That is what we are discussing.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
And I say to the minister that the discrimination which has been kept on our statute books still remains, when the Chinese resident of Canada is put on a different basis from the resident of any other alien nationality in this country. There is a discrimination.
The minister says to me that I would do this, that and the other thing. I put it squarely up to the minister: How does he propose to remove this discrimination? It is all very well for us to talk in the house about oriental immigration, or all the rest of it, which does not come under this bill. But let me remind hon. gentlemen that the day is past when any nation, whatever its colour, can look down upon any other nation, and treat the nationals of that country as an inferior people.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Does that apply to Spain?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
It applies to every
country of the world.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Then why did you want to keep them out of UNO?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Why did we want to keep Spain out of UNO?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Because UNO is an organization of democratic peace-loving [DOT]countries. And so long as Francisco Franco remains dictator of Spain, is it right to call Spain a democratic country or a peace-loving country?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: It is racial and religious discrimination.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I will not enter into a controversy with the hon. member regarding Spain, because Spain does not come under this bill.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: According to you.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: But I am quite willing to enter into a discussion with my hon. friend as to what constitutes democracy.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: That is what you say.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: And as to what constitutes justice among the people of a nation.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Are you the supreme judge?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I do not accept race hatred, as it is preached by some people in the United States, and their fellow travellers in the Dominion of Canada.
But what I was saying was this, that my objection to this particular measure-and I am going to support it, because it does go a considerable way toward removing discrimination-my objection to an aspect of this measure is that it does not remove discrimination that should be removed at this time.
We are members of the united nations organization. We have removed several skeletons from the Canadian cupboard lately, when the province of British Columbia removed disabilities against East Indians and Chinese, in the matter of the franchise. Those skeletons have been removed from our cupboard, I am thankful to say. But so long as any vestige of racial discrimination remains, we are open to attack in the united nations organization, because we are not carrying out the principles upon which that organization was founded.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Does he believe that the control of immigration is a matter for a country itself-and in our instance, Canada -or does he think the united nations organization has authority over immigration into Canada?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I shall answer that clearly and concisely. The united nations organization has no authority to decide anything that we shall do within the sphere of our domestic jurisdiction. But we have a moral obligation when we sign a charter guaranteeing human rights and fundamental freedoms, when we pledge our word to remove discrimination on account of race, creed or colour.
I say to my hon. friend the member for Vancouver South that I agree, immediately, that this country has a right to decide upon its immigration policy. But I say to my hon. friend also that no liberal-and I use the

Immigration Act
term in the proper sense, with a small "1", and not in a political sense-can possibly condone any policy based upon racial discrimination. That is what I say. No liberal, no man who calls himself a liberal, can possibly condone a policy which is founded upon racial discrimination, discrimination on account of race, or creed or of colour.
The bill before us is a very simple bill and, since it removes certain disabilities, we are going to support it. But I say to my hon. friend that, had the government been consistent and followed the policy which we understood the Prime Minister laid down in his statement when he said that all discrimination would be removed, then all residents in Canada-that is all we are talking about- whether they be of Czech origini, or Scandinavian origin or of any other origin, would be at liberty to bring in their wives and children under eighteen years as they may do now and would be in exactly the same position as residents of Chinese origin. In other words, if we allow Czech, the Swede, the Norwegian or any other national resident in this country to bring in his wife and children, then the resident of Chinese origin should be accorded the same privilege if wre are removing all vestiges of discrimination as the Prime Minister indicated. That is the point I am making.
To the minister who turns to me and says, "What would you do?" I say, "What are you going to do to remove this vestige of discrimination?" What is he going to do to remove this blight on the escutcheon of Canada? What is he going to do to justify the calling of that government over there a Liberal government. Liberalism once stood for something very different from that which is included in. this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I am greatly thrilled
indeed to have a lecture on Liberalism from an arch socialist in this house. I want to tell him that I was raised in the cradle of Liberalism and I have been a Liberal all my life. He has not met the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who referred to the possibility of a great preponderance of population of another race coming into our province of British Columbia with only a million people. We have to face this question not only as a nation but as a province which must consider the proper preponderance in order to keep the herd pure, in order to keep the old Anglo-Saxon-French balance and the central European balance proper in this country. When he talks about Liberalism to me, my goodness, it is the biggest insult I ever had in this house.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
He
was talking to a member of the herd.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I have reason to
believe that my hon. friend was once tinged with Toryism, that he was possibly a Tory, but now he is a red-hot, fire-brand socialist. We over here are Liberal reformers; we believe in the essential idealism of Liberalism; we believe in the essential principles of liberty and freedom; we believe in the dominance of the white race in the Dominion of Canada, and for that we stand.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I was objecting at the beginning to the introduction of something other than the clauses of this bill tonight. The hon. gentleman has astutely taken the opportunity to reply to me, but he forgets the issue. I am putting the question to the hon. member-

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I will speak again.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: So will I.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: -as was stated by two of his followers this afternoon, that he believed and that they believed, that their argument was that immigration should be brought under P.C. 695 with the deletion of the clause regarding Asiatics. Is that the position the hon. member is taking?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Yes, but not with your interpretation of that position. Do not try to twist what we are saying. W'e want the removal of racial discrimination in so far as that order in council goes. You know where the discrimination is as well as I do.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
The question that was asked
of those two hon. members was:	Are you
proposing to repeal order in council 2115, and the answer was, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: They said so.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: The repeal of order in council 2115 would place immigration under the regulation of order in council 695. I asked them if they proposed to take the clause dealing with Asiatics out of P.C. 695. and the answer was. yes. That means that the law and the regulations governing immigration into this country, if their wishes were acceded to, would be under P.C. 695, and then any person resident in Canada could bring in his father, his mother, his brother and every one of the denominations in the categories that are included in 695. That is where you would be.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Why not?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Can other races do the same thing?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: All the Chinese who have been legally admitted to Canada would be in the same position as the Swedish or other people.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Also agriculturists.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I read to the house the statement the hon. member made with regard to the assimilability of these people. He said that the acid test of assimilability is intermarriage, but that neither the Chinese nor the Indian governments favour intermarriage of their nationals coming to Canada.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I said that, yes.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: The hon. member stated, I think positively, that they will not assimilate with our Canadian people. Therefore he wishes a gentleman's agreement. That is not what was said today.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: It is what I said.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Your two followers did not say that.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Do you agree with everything in every particular that individuals behind you say?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
Your followers said today
that they wanted immigration under P.C. 695; yet in the interview you gave you said that the acid test of assimilability is intermarriage, but that neither the Chinese nor the Indian governments favour intermarriage of their nationals coming to Canada.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I say that the acid test of any nation's non-discriminatory policy is equality. You are trying to dodge the question: What will you do?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Exactly what this bill is doing.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Then you do not remove discrimination.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: We take the position, as was stated by the Prime Minister, that Canada recognizes the right of all other countries to control the entry or non-entry of persons seeking to become permanent residents and that we claim precisely the same right for our country. That is the position I am taking.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
We have heard a lot about racial discrimination as applied to orientals and the people outside Canada, but I should like to take up the case of racial discrimination against the oldest citizens of Canada. I ask the leader of the C.C.F. to answer this
question: Is it not the fact that Indians in this country are not allowed to consume alcoholic beverages as white men are?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Order. I would remind the hon. member that we are dealing with section 2, which relates to the ' repeal of section 80 of the Immigration Act. That refers to the Chinese only.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I was merely giving an illustration of racial discrimination, and I wanted to hear the answer of the leader of the C.C.F. on this particular aspect of racial discrimination. I state the fact that the Indians as a race, and for no other reason than that they are of the Indian race, are not allowed to take a drink the same as I am allowed to take a drink, or as the leader of the C.C.F. is allowed to take a drink; and I ask the leader of the C.C.F. whether he would advocate that Indians be allowed to drink as freely as he and I are allowed to do, andi if not, why not?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this has nothing to do with the matter.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: It is an example of racial discrimination.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I will, however, answer the question. The way in which the Indians in this country have been treated has been a blot on Canada's good name.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is correct when he says that the question has nothing to do with the section under consideration.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
We have been making a great fuss over who is going to flood the country and who is going to have a dirink and who is not, and I think it is time that we got down to a reasonable understanding of the issues involved. If the Chinese are put on the same basis as other people so far as their right to enter this country is concerned, that does not mean that Canada must allow the entry of every Chinese who comes within the regulations and asks to come here. We do not admit everybody from other countries who comes within the regulations. It is pretty difficult, as a matter of fact, for any person of any race who does come within the regulations to enter Canada now. There is, I suppose, no discrimination against Poles entering this country. As a matter of fact, quite a number of them entered Canada fairly easily not so long ago. Yet I have been making inquiries on behalf of a. Canadian citizen who fought in the last war and whose daughter was in Great Britain during the war and married a Polish soldier. This Canadian citizen wants to
Immigration Act

bring his daughter and son-in-law to Canada but he cannot. If we can apply restrictions of that kind to Poles why cannot we apply them to the Chinese without being charged with discrimination? We certainly can make what laws we like, but these laws should apply equally to peoples of all nations. If the Minister of Mines and Resources says that he does not agree with that, he is repudiating the statement which the Prime Minister made in January, that wTe were removing all discrimination. You cannot remove discrimination and at the same time maintain it.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
How would you reduce the number of the Chinese who may come in? If you say that any agricultural labourer may come in, how are you going to keep the Chinese out?
Mr. MaeINNIS: I do not think anjr agricultural labourer from any other country ryho wants to come to Canada can come in now. If they can, very few of them are coming in. With the removal of all discrimination there is no reason in the world why conditions cannot be made that will limit the number of Chinese, coming into this country in proportion to the numbers of any other race entering the country.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
That is quite different.
Mr. MaeINNIS: It is not different at all.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member is speaking of a quota system?
Mr. MaeINNIS: I am speaking of a quota system. If the removal of discrimination requires a quota system, then let us have a quota system, but do not let us shout to the world that we are removing discrimination While at the same time we are maintaining it.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
The minister made reference to my remarks this afternoon and I feel that he did not draw effective conclusions. I will repeat again what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said. On January 27 the Prime Minister promised this country and the world that, so far as Canada was concerned, the effect of the repeal would be to remove all discrimination against the Chinese on account of race and to bring the Chinese under the general provisions of the Immigration Act and no longer under legislation applying exclusively to people of Chinese origin.
The minister has said that the government is going back on that promise of the Prime Minister, that it is not the intention to remove racial discrimination. I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that normally quite a number of Canadians go to China as merchants or as missionaries. We would think

it unreasonable of the Chinese government if they insisted that every Canadian who went to China should become a citizen of that country before being permitted to bring in his wife and children, and naturally the people of China consider it unreasonable that we have one law for the Chinese and another for Europeans.
It was mentioned earlier tonight that the United States was still discriminating against the Chinese, but according to my information the United States in 1943 repealed their Chinese exclusion act. The president of the day, the late President Roosevelt, is quoted as saying:
China's resistance does not depend alone on guns and planes and on attacks on land, on the sea and from the air. It is based as much on the spirit of her people and her faith in her allies. We owe it to the Chinese to strengthen that faith. One step in this direction is to wipe from the statute books those anachronisms in our law which forbid the immigration of Chinese people into this country and which bar Chinese residents from American citizenship.
That was in 1943. If P.C. 695 does not meet with the approval of the administration I think it is imperative that an order in council be drafted immediately which will be acceptable to the government and which will remove completely any discrimination on account of race or religion. I make this last plea with the minister to repeal P.C. 2115, and, if he cannot accept P.C. 695 with the last paragraph struck out, that he amend it to place all people in the same position because, as the hon. member for Vancouver East has pointed out, it would not mean that every applicant would be accepted. The administration would still have the authority to decide who should be admitted. But we cannot go to the united nations meeting with this sort of regulation in effect in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to put one more simple question to the minister. Those of us who have been talking about this question in the house and those who have been writing editorials about it have tried to focus attention on what amounts to one pretty small group. I am not going back on any of the general statements I have made, but we are talking now of one small specific group, namely, Chinese persons resident in Canada who are not citizens, and our suggestion is that Chinese persons legally resident in Canada who are not citizens should have the same right as European persons legally resident in Canada. We made our suggestion as to how that right should be extended to them, the right to bring in their wives and children. The minister objected to our way of doing it on the ground that it was opening the doors

Immigration Act
too wide. Other members of this group have made an answer to that and I am not going into it farther.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: What was the answer? I did not get the answer, if there was one.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am not going to take up the time to give it again. It is on the record from the leader of this group and from the hon. member for Vancouver East. I am really trying to narrow this down to the specific group which most of us are immediately concerned about. What I am saying is that if the minister does not approve the way that we suggest doing it, on the ground that it opens the doors too far, has he not some suggestion to meet this particular group? Is there not some way in which he can provide for Chinese residents now resident in Canada, whether citizens or not, by permitting them to bring in their wives, just as European persons do who are resident in Canada and who do not happen to be citizens? One answer that he might make is that they can become citizens. That is admitting that he is prepared to have that number come in. Why not remove from the statute books that racial discrimination with respect to these people? Has he any suggestion?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: As I understand the hon. member's question, he is asking that I should consent to P.C. 695 being applicable to Chinese in the same way as it is applicable to anyone else. Because of the argument that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was adducing in the house when he was speaking and also the hon. member for Mackenzie, I asked the specific question whether that was their argument. That would mean that under P.C. 695 the Chinese would have the same rights as Europeans to come into this country and in a year bring in their wives under certain conditions and all the other categories of relatives. Does the hon. gentleman seriously mean that I should consent to such an amendment.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: We are hot asking that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
I am sure the minister must have misunderstood the question I was putting to him, for he asked me this question before and I gave him my answer categorically without any hesitation. I have accepted the fact that we cannot agree on that, and I am trying to see now if there is not some point between his position and mine to which the government might move. I am trying to ask him if there is not some way, in an amended form of P.C. 695, if you like, by means of which provision can be made just for Chinese 83166-178
persons resident in Canada, whether citizens or not, to bring in their wives and children.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I should not like to say that there was. At the moment I would not care to say that we could meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am asking the government to give consideration to that point.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I should like to recall to the committee a matter which I brought to the attention of the house some days ago. If we allow a sufficient number of Chinese to come into British Columbia to become the predominating element I should like members of the C.C.F. to tell us how we should be able to prevent discrimination against the white people in British Columbia.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
Why pick on British
Columbia?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Because it is an illustration. Hon. members have simple minds. I am trying to get the matter down so that they can get hold of it. Hon. members of the committee must bear this in mind. We must prevent the white race from being discriminated against, and particularly the Anglo-Saxons. It is a simple matter for us to put so many people into this country who are not of our particular way of life as would make it impossible for us to have a chance to live.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
What about the
F rench-Canadians ?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: All right; I shall put them in too. You can get so many Chinese and Japanese into this country that the ordinary Canadian, French or British would not have any chance to live according to the standard of life to which they are accustomed. If anyone pretends that a situation such as that would not be discriminating against our own people I should like to see him rise in his place and give his reasons for his belief. This is a matter which needs to be faced.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I assume that the transportation system on the Pacific is just as bad as it is on the Atlantic.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Worse.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext:
Very well. That strengthens the argument I am going to advance. Within a year Chinese residents in Canada can take out citizenship papers. Then they are entitled to bring their wives and children under eighteen years of age to this country. If we grant them that right now as residents, with the situation on the Pacific being as bad as it is on the

Immigration Act

Atlantic, they will not be able to bring these relatives of theirs into this country for more than a year. Therefore, why maintain this discrimination against them? Will the minister please answer?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I do not know what the question is, really.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: It is a statement of fact, that if we grant that same equality of right to the Chinese residents in Canada that we do to other residents, because of the nature of things in the shipping world they cannot bring their relatives to Canada within a year or two. If we permit them to take out citizenship, as we shall, I assume, they will do so by the time the year has expired. Then they will have the right to bring their families here. We are making no difference at all so far as immigration into this country within a year is concerned. Why then continue this discrimination?

Section agreed to.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Since we are now off the Chinese question for the time being, I should like to bring up the matter of the transportation of dependents of ex-service men to the country. Can the minister tell us what arrangements are being made for the transportation of such of these dependents as are still overseas? What space is being secured'? When are these people to be able to get over here?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am informed that they must apply for their own space in order to get here.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Does the Canadian government make no arrangements so far as space for these people is concerned? Does it not aid them in seeming space?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Up to the end of last year they did, but not now. There is no provision made for it now.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I should like to urge upon the minister that arrangements be made to secure space for these people, and in addition to the particular dependents who are mentioned in this section, that aid be given to secure space for the categories of people I mentioned this afternoon, fiancees of returned men and close relatives, mothers, brothers, sisters, fathers, and so forth. I do not think we shall be able to say that we have solved the problem of bringing these dependents of ex-service personnel to this country until these people are over here.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that a committee is now functioning in England under the chairmanship, I think, of Mr. Norman Robertson, considering all these related questions with reference to transportation of relatives and dependents of ex-service men.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I should like to know how the thing is functioning. Is it actually getting these people over? I mentioned the case of the fiancee of one of these men of ours who has been trying now for well over a year to get the girl over, but she is still in England. What is actually being done?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: There never was any provision for fiancees.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am urging that there should be.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA

That is one of our
hardships.

speechtext: I have a question to ask. The minister gave figures of 77,000 tonight. Can he say how many of these include dependents such as are covered in this bill, and fiancees and brides of Canadian soldiers who returned to Canada?

No, Mr. Chairman.
There is one other matter I wish to take up in connection with this. It is the case of men who were married before the war started, whose wives were caught over in Europe-in England, or wherever the case may be-and who, because of the particular wording of subsection 4 (b) of this particular act, are not included. I asked this afternoon if the minister, when we came to take up this section, would say whether anything would be done for those people. I instanced particularly the case of a man whose wife was caught in Belgium, who

Immigration Act
had great difficulty in getting her back after the war, and who had to pay for her himself. I expressed my idea that wives and children of men who did serve overseas should have the same privilege as wives who were secure whilst the men were over there. Has the minister anything to say in that connection?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: I am afraid I am not in a position to help them. There are many in the same category as those the hon. gentleman speaks of where the expense had to be borne by somebody but not by the government. I am afraid I cannot do anything to help in that connection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA

No, Mr. Chairman. In that event I should like to move a small amendment: in line 29, after the world "while", insert the words "or before". The subsection would then- read:
The wife or widow of a member of the forces who is not resident in Canada and who was married to such member of the forces while or before such member of the forces was serving outside of Canada or the territorial waters thereof . . .
And so on. I offer that amendment in order to protect those people, however many there are-I do not suppose the number is very great, but there is a great hardship on those who are in that situation-and to bring them within the meaning of this act.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: No. This would mean an addition to the amounts that might be provided, so far as I can see it just now; and I am afraid that I could not accept that amendment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister has got the point?

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
speechtext: Oh, oh.

Why should that 'be? This husband served five years over there and he fought all through northwestern Europe. Apparently I have used a wrong
expression somewhere, Mr. Chairman. That does seem to me to be a reasonable change which is asked for.

subtopic: REPEAL OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT-BONDING OF PERSONS IN TRANSIT THROUGH CANADA
